title: Opal and the Monster Who Could Lose
subtitle: Opal’s secret challenge teaches her something unexpected.
editorialNote: New story adapted from a recovered plot summary; original wording was unavailable.

paragraphs: After three successful adventures in a row, Axey decided that the friends could win absolutely anything.
“Anything?” Lolo asked.
“Anything.”
“Even a race against a cloud?”
“Especially a cloud. No feet.”
Opal smiled, but she wondered what would happen when a puzzle did not open or a race did not end with a trophy. She decided to invent a challenge the friends could not win on their first try.
Unique Pink helped make a soft purple monster costume. It had floppy ears, a crooked grin, and pockets big enough for biscuits. They placed a pretend Opal on a cushion with a book across her lap.
Lolo studied the pretend girl. “You should tell them afterward.”
“I will,” Opal promised.
The monster appeared beside the cushion bridge and announced a contest.
“Cross my bridge before I count to three!”
Axey leaped forward. “One!” the monster cried. “Two! Three!”
He had barely reached the first cushion.
“Again,” Axey said.
Again the monster counted too fast. Again nobody reached the other side.
Langston planted his hands on his hips. “I object. I am an expert in ridiculous competitions, and this one is suspicious.”
The monster challenged Finley to find a hidden ribbon. But each time Finley got close, the monster moved it.
Stella stopped wagging her tail.
“This doesn't feel very fun.”

illustration.alt: Opal holds her sloth lovey Lolo while reading inside the purple galaxy tent.

paragraphs: Inside the costume, Opal's smile faded. She had wanted to teach everyone something. Instead, she was making up rules they could not possibly follow.
Lolo walked to the bridge.
“Monster,” she said gently, “does losing mean the game was fair?”
Opal thought of the ribbon moving from one pocket to another.
“No,” she admitted in her monster voice.
“And does being upset about an unfair game mean somebody is bad at losing?”
Opal sat down. One floppy ear fell across her face.
“No.”
She took off the costume's head.
“Opal!” Axey gasped. Then he looked back at the cushion. “But you're also over there!”
Langston examined the pretend Opal. “That explains why she didn't laugh at my joke. I was beginning to question the joke.”
Opal told everyone what she had planned.
“I thought you needed practice losing. But I didn't ask you, and I didn't make the game fair. I'm sorry.”
Axey sat beside her. “I did say we could win anything.”
“You're allowed to be excited,” Lolo told him. “And you're allowed to feel disappointed when things are hard.”
Together they rebuilt the challenge. Coatl made a stable bridge. Cinny wrote clear rules. Finley hid the ribbon once and promised not to move it.
Opal asked to go first.
She searched beneath the wrong cushion. Then another. When the timer finished, she had not found the ribbon.
For a moment she wanted to say the timer was too fast.
Instead she took a breath.
“I feel cross,” she said.
“Would you like a hug or another try?” Lolo asked.
“A hug. Then another try.”
On her next turn, Opal noticed a golden thread caught on a cushion seam. It led to the ribbon.

Axey did not finish the bridge course on his first attempt. Stella walked beside him while he practiced. Langston knocked over a stack of soft cups with his elbow and announced that his elbow was entering separately next time.
Nobody won every game. Everybody got another chance.
When evening came, Opal hung the monster costume beside the tent flap.
“Should we keep her?” she asked.
“Yes,” Axey said. “But next time she has to follow the rules.”
Langston put the floppy monster head on his knee.
“Finally. A worthy opponent for somebody else's knees.”
Lolo laughed, and Opal reached for her hand.
The End.
